deep.reconstruction:
Setup (sphere of radius r, centre O, pole N). Two maps of a point X at polar distance θ (angle NOX) and azimuth ω are drawn in one figure with common centre C, the image of the pole N.

(a) Stereographic projection from the opposite pole S onto the equatorial plane: X ↦ r·tan(θ/2)·e^{iω}. Its scale at the pole is 1/2.

(b) Central (gnomonic) projection from O onto the tangent plane at N, translated so that N falls on C: X ↦ r·tan θ·e^{iω}. Its scale at the pole is 1.

This is the meaning of 'Maassstab für jene im Pol C halb so gross als für diese'.

The circle of radius r about C (through A and B) is therefore:
- for the stereographic map, θ = 90°, the equator;
- for the central map, tan θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°, the 45° parallel.

P and Q are the stereographic and central images of the same point X. Both lie on the ray from C in direction ω, so C, P, Q are collinear. A is chosen on the circle with CA ⟂ CPQ. Then (my explicit step):
- CP = r·tan(θ/2), so angle CAP = θ/2;
- CQ = r·tan θ, so angle CAQ = θ;
- hence angle CAP = angle PAQ: AP bisects angle CAQ.

This gives a ruler-and-compass conversion of one map into the other.

Antipode. Draw AD ⟂ AP with D on the line QPC produced beyond C. Then angle CAD = 90° − θ/2, so CD = r·cot(θ/2) = r·tan((180°−θ)/2), on the side opposite P. The antipode of X has polar distance 180°−θ and azimuth ω+180°, so D is its stereographic image. In complex form, z_D = −r²/conj(z_P).

Polar great circle. The great circle whose pole is X meets the meridian of X at signed polar angles θ ± 90°. Their stereographic images are r·tan(θ/2 ± 45°) along the line CPQ.
- With t = tan(θ/2), the sum is tan(θ/2+45°) + tan(θ/2−45°) = 4t/(1−t²) = 2·tan θ, so the image circle's centre is at r·tan θ, i.e. at Q.
- Its radius is (r/2)(tan(θ/2+45°) − tan(θ/2−45°)) = r(1+t²)/(1−t²) = r·sec θ = QA.
- So the image is the circle about Q through A (and B). This is consistent with the great circle meeting the equator at the two points 90° in azimuth from X's meridian, which are A and B.

The next page (238) states the same relation analytically. If z_c = a+bi is the central image, the stereographic image is z_s = z_c·r·(√(|z_c|²+r²) − r)/|z_c|². This follows from tan(θ/2) = (sec θ − 1)/tan θ with tan θ = |z_c|/r.
errors: No mathematical errors found. 'AD normal gegen PA' and 'D auf der verlängerten QPC' are correct, with D lying beyond C on the side opposite P and Q. In the figure D is drawn far above C (the side opposite P and Q), consistent with CD = r·cot(θ/2), which is large for a point near the pole.
Implicit, unstated assumption: the gnomonic image is translated into the equatorial plane so that both pole images coincide at C, and both radii equal r.

results.what: Geometric link between stereographic (from the antipodal pole onto the equatorial plane) and gnomonic projection: AP bisects angle CAQ, because tan(θ/2) is the half-angle of tan θ.
results.modern_name: Relation between stereographic and gnomonic projections via the half-angle (tangent half-angle) formula
results.usually_credited_to: Classical: the projections go back to Hipparchus/Ptolemy and Thales; the half-angle relation is folklore in cartography (Lambert's era and earlier)

results.what: Construction of the stereographic image of the antipodal point: D with AD ⟂ AP, i.e. z_D = −r²/conj(z_P).
The stereographic image of the great circle with pole X is the circle centred at the gnomonic image Q of X, with radius QA = r·sec θ.
results.modern_name: Image of a great circle under stereographic projection (circle preservation), centred at the gnomonic image of its pole
results.usually_credited_to: Circle preservation: Ptolemy/Jordanus, Harriot; this specific centre characterisation is standard in crystallographic and astronomical projection practice

deep.surprise_reason: This is elegant but elementary projective/spherical geometry, known in cartography and astronomy before Gauss. It is a neat private note with no new result.

checkable.asserts: angle CAQ = 2·angle CAP, i.e. CQ = r·tan θ when CP = r·tan(θ/2) (equals 0)
the centre of the stereographic image of the polar great circle is at the gnomonic image Q (equals 0)
the radius of that image circle is sec θ = QA (equals 0)
CD = r·cot(θ/2) is the stereographic distance of the antipode, polar angle π−θ (equals 0)
Gauss's p.238 formula maps the central image r·tan θ to the stereographic image r·tan(θ/2) (evaluates to 0 for 0<θ<π/2, r>0)

transcription_corrections: 'im Pol{+C+}' should read 'im Pol C': C is an interlinear insertion naming the pole's image.
'gegenüber liegende' should be 'gegenüber liegenden' (the ending is cramped but present: 'des jenem Kugelpunkte gegenüber liegenden').
